html:
An empire based in Bengal and Bihar, in eastern India, ruled by the Buddhist Pala dynasty from the mid 8th to the 12th century. Its kings were the last great royal patrons of Buddhism in India.

It began with an election. After decades of chaos, which a later inscription calls "the law of the fish" (the big eating the small), the chiefs of Bengal chose a leader named Gopala as king around 750. His son Dharmapala and grandson Devapala, in the late 8th and early 9th centuries, made the Palas the strongest power in north India for a time. They fought for the city of Kannauj in a long three-way struggle with the Gurjara-Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas. Their army was known for its war elephants, and their fleet sailed the Bay of Bengal.

Buddhist learning flourished under them:

  • They supported Nalanda and founded new monasteries, such as Vikramashila and Somapura, whose ruins in Bangladesh are a World Heritage Site.
  • Vajrayana, the tantric form of Buddhism, developed in their monasteries.
  • Pala bronze sculpture and illustrated palm-leaf manuscripts shaped the art of Nepal, Tibet and Southeast Asia.
  • A king of Srivijaya in Sumatra paid for a monastery at Nalanda, and Devapala granted villages for its upkeep.
  • The teacher Atisha left Vikramashila for Tibet in 1040, where he helped revive Buddhism.

From the 11th century the Palas weakened, troubled by revolts and by a raid from the Chola Empire around 1020. The Hindu Sena dynasty replaced them in the 12th century. Soon after 1200 Turkish armies of the new Delhi Sultanate overran Bihar and Bengal and the great monasteries were destroyed.
sum: An empire based in Bengal and Bihar, in eastern India, ruled by the Buddhist Pala dynasty from the mid 8th to the 12th century. Its kings were the last great royal patrons of Buddhism in India.
